notes.meaning: Large merchant ships returning from distant voyages are told to weep because the great port of Tyre is in ruins. The docks and homes have been wiped out, leaving no safe harbor for sailors to enter. The crews first hear this shocking report when they stop at the island of Cyprus.

The people along the coast and on the island of Tyre are told to be silent in shock. The noisy markets and busy sea traders from nearby Sidon once filled this city with people and riches. Now all that bustling noise has been silenced by God's judgment.

Tyre built its wealth by shipping and selling grain grown along the Nile river in Egypt. Phoenician ships carried these huge harvests across the Mediterranean Sea to feed many nations. The city became the great marketplace of the ancient world.

Sidon, the older parent city of the region, is told to feel deep shame over Tyre's fall. The island fortress of Tyre now cries out like a mother who has lost all her children. War has swept away her young men and women, leaving her completely barren and lonely.

Egypt will shudder with dread when news comes that Tyre has fallen. The Egyptians relied heavily on Tyre to sell their crops and protect sea trade. They will realize that if such a strong fortress can be destroyed, their own land is in grave danger.

The survivors in Tyre are urged to escape across the sea to distant colonies like Tarshish. They had sailed those waters before as proud merchants, but now they must flee as homeless refugees. The coastland people can only wail at how completely their secure world has vanished.

The prophet contrasts Tyre's old pride with its sudden misery. The city was famous for its ancient beginnings and its joy, sending out travelers to build colonies far away. Now its pampered citizens must walk on foot into captivity and exile.

A question is asked about who could possibly bring down such a grand city. Tyre was so powerful that it gave out crowns to rulers of other lands, and its traders were treated like kings and princes. From a human viewpoint, its sudden collapse seemed impossible.

The Lord Almighty is the one who decided to bring ruin upon Tyre. He did this to stain their proud beauty and humble all who boast in their own greatness. God brings low the pride of this world to show that all earthly glory is temporary.

The distant colony of Tarshish is told that it is finally free from Tyre's tight control. Tyre no longer has the strength or the fleet to restrain its colonies or force them to pay tribute. Like the Nile river spreading across the land after a flood, the people of Tarshish can now roam and work their own land freely.

The Lord has raised His hand over the sea and made surrounding kingdoms tremble in fear. He issued the royal command to shatter the strongholds of Phoenicia. No sea wall or fortress can stand once God commands its destruction.

God declares that Tyre's carefree celebration has come to an end. The city had never been conquered before and lived like an untouched virgin, but now it is crushed by enemy forces. Even if the people flee across the water to Cyprus, they will find no peaceful resting place from trouble.

The people are told to look at the Babylonians, or Chaldeans, as a sobering lesson. They were once simple desert wanderers of no great renown, yet God made them strong enough to build siege towers and tear down proud palaces. If powerful kingdoms can be brought to ruin by an unexpected foe, Tyre should not have trusted in its own wealth.

The opening cry of the poem is repeated to the great trading vessels of Tarshish. They are told to weep because the port city that gave them wealth, safety, and business has been reduced to rubble. With their main harbor destroyed, their livelihood is completely gone.

Tyre will lie neglected and forgotten for seventy years, matching the length of the Babylonian empire. When that seventy-year period ends, the city will begin to revive and seek out trade once more. It will act like an aging singer trying to get people to remember her name.

The prophet quotes from a well-known song about an old, forgotten prostitute. She is told to take her harp, walk the streets, and sing pleasant songs so that men will pay attention to her again. In the same way, Tyre will use lively schemes, fine goods, and sweet talk to entice foreign merchants back to its markets.

After the seventy years are over, the Lord will show mercy and allow Tyre to rebuild its trading power. However, the city will return to its old habits and trade greedily with every nation on earth. Scripture compares this purely money-driven commerce to prostitution because it sells its soul to anyone for quick gain.

A day will come when the profits of Tyre are dedicated directly to the Lord instead of hoarded for selfish luxury. Its wealth will be given to provide abundant food and good clothing for those who serve God. This began to take shape when Tyrians helped rebuild Jerusalem's temple and later when many of them turned to faith in Christ.
